assumptions.assumption: Farm near Ely, Cambridgeshire (about 52.40 N, 0.26 E), on East Anglian Fen deep peat; DT8 Fenland parameters apply to the 100 ha of potatoes and wheat, and the DT6 'fens' pilot tile stands in for the farm's hedgerow-tree growth.
assumptions.rationale: Ely sits in the Fens, which DT8 and the DT6 fens pilot cover.

assumptions.assumption: The 80 ha of grass is treated as not on drained deep peat, so no peat-soil CO2/N2O is calculated for it; only the livestock methane is counted.
assumptions.rationale: The user said only the potato and wheat ground is deep peat.

assumptions.assumption: The arable peat is at the DT8 drained Fenland climatology (mean water table about 0.66 m below the surface), with typical Fenland fertiliser rates.

Two readings: (a) keep growing potatoes with the mean water table raised to 0.45 m and to 0.30 m; (b) fully rewet the 60 ha to reed paludiculture, with a sweep of water tables (0.05-0.66 m) after an established regime (3 years).
assumptions.rationale: 'Raising the water table' could mean partial raising under cropping or full rewetting; both are shown.

assumptions.assumption: 90 suckler cows with followers = 90 beef cows, 2 breeding bulls, 85 calves, 20 breeding heifers, 40 steers and 20 heifers for slaughter; 200 ewes with 5 rams and 300 lambs.
assumptions.rationale: Typical suckler herd with about 95% calving and 20% replacement; about 1.5 lambs per ewe. The user did not give follower numbers.

assumptions.assumption: Applied to cattle only, as a herd-average enteric reduction of 15% (central: about 30% effect while housed for about half the year) and 30% (upper: effect all year). No additive for grazing sheep.
assumptions.rationale: Methane-reducing additives are mainly fed in housed rations; suckler cattle graze much of the year.

assumptions.assumption: About 3 km of hedge with one new hedgerow tree every 30 m = 100 trees planted in 2027, followed for 50 years.
CO2-equivalents use AR6 GWP100 throughout (DT8 uses AR6; DT2 set to AR6 for consistency).
assumptions.rationale: So that the different sources can be added up.

input.title: Your Ely farm: where the emissions come from, and what three options would do
input.audience: A tenant farmer near Ely (180 ha: potatoes and wheat on deep peat, grass, suckler cows and ewes)
input.question_as_understood: Where do most of the greenhouse-gas emissions on a 180 ha tenanted farm near Ely come from? The farm has 60 ha of potatoes and 40 ha of winter wheat on deep peat, 80 ha of grass, 90 suckler cows with followers, 200 breeding ewes and a few kilometres of hedges. And how much would each of these change emissions: (1) raising the water table on the potato ground, (2) a methane-reducing feed additive, (3) planting hedgerow trees?
key_findings: The drained peat is by far the biggest source. The 100 ha of potatoes and wheat give off about 3,710 t CO2e a year: about 37 t CO2e per hectare, mostly CO2 from the peat breaking down [R1, R2]. That is roughly 88% of the farm total we could model.

Methane from the livestock comes to about 504 t CO2e a year (18.7 t of methane). About 87% of that comes from the cattle and 13% from the sheep. Nearly all of it comes from digestion (enteric methane) rather than manure [R6].

Raising the water table on the 60 ha of potatoes is the biggest lever. If you keep growing potatoes, raising the yearly average water table from about 0.66 m to 0.45 m below the surface cuts about 770 t CO2e a year, and raising it to 0.30 m cuts about 1,410 t. Rewetting the land to grow reed at about 0.20 m cuts about 2,100 t a year [R1, R3–R5].
A feed additive fed to the cattle cuts about 59 t CO2e a year if it works out at a 15% herd-average reduction, or about 118 t at 30%. That is about 1.5–3% of the farm total [R6–R8].
100 new hedgerow trees would take up on average about 0.4–1.0 t CO2 a year over 50 years, or 18–48 t in total over that time [R9]. That is small for climate, but trees can do other jobs on the farm.
input.results_markdown:
**Today: the farm's modelled emissions (AR6 GWP100, t CO2e per year)**

| Source | Per ha or per farm | Farm total |
|---|---|---|
| Potatoes on drained peat (60 ha) | 36.99 t/ha: CO2 29.77, N2O 7.25, CH4 ≈ 0 [R1] | ≈ 2,219 |
| Winter wheat on drained peat (40 ha) | 37.34 t/ha: CO2 33.07, N2O 4.27 [R2] | ≈ 1,493 |
| Cattle methane (90 cows, 2 bulls, 85 calves, 80 youngstock) | 16.3 t CH4 | ≈ 439 |
| Sheep methane (200 ewes, 5 rams, 300 lambs) | 2.4 t CH4 | ≈ 65 |
| **Total that could be modelled** | | **≈ 4,217** |

Farm totals are the per-hectare figures multiplied by your areas, or the livestock figures split by category [R6]. Livestock methane totals 18.68 t CH4 = 504.5 t CO2e; 16.86 t of the methane comes from digestion and 1.82 t from manure. The peat soils assume the drained Fenland water table (yearly average about 0.66 m below the surface) and 200 kg N/ha of fertiliser.

**Option 1: raise the water table on the 60 ha of potatoes**

| Water level (yearly average depth) | Net t CO2e/ha/yr | Saving on 60 ha (t CO2e/yr) |
|---|---|---|
| Potatoes, today's drainage (0.66 m) [R1] | 36.99 | 0 |
| Potatoes, 0.45 m (still drawn down in summer) [R3] | 24.21 | ≈ 767 |
| Potatoes, 0.30 m (still drawn down in summer) [R4] | 13.44 | ≈ 1,413 |
| Rewet to reed, 0.30 m [R5] | 5.54 | ≈ 1,887 |
| Rewet to reed, 0.20 m (lowest net emissions found) [R5] | 1.97 | ≈ 2,101 |
| Rewet to reed, 0.05 m [R5] | 2.79 | ≈ 2,052 |

As the water rises, CO2 falls sharply and the land releases a little more methane. Under reed at 0.20 m, methane is 1.04 t CO2e/ha. When the water reaches the surface (0.05 m), methane rises to 4.27 t, which is why the very wettest setting is slightly worse than 0.20 m [R5].

**Option 2: methane-reducing feed additive (cattle only)**
- 15% herd-average cut in methane from digestion: 445.7 t CO2e, a saving of about 59 t/yr [R7].
- 30% herd-average cut: 387.0 t CO2e, a saving of about 118 t/yr [R8].
- Sheep are not included, because grazing ewes are not fed a ration that could carry an additive.

**Option 3: 100 hedgerow trees (about one every 30 m along 3 km)**
The model used growth measured from lidar for hedgerow trees in the Fens. About 85% of trees survive establishment, and about 71 of the 100 are still alive after 40 years. Over 50 years the trees take up 18 t CO2 (range 8–35) with one growth model and 48 t CO2 (range 33–64) with the other [R9]. By about 2066, uptake reaches roughly 0.6–1.4 t CO2 a year.
input.interpretation_markdown:
**What drives your footprint.** Almost nine-tenths of your modelled emissions come from the peat itself, not from what you grow or graze on it. Draining keeps the water table about two-thirds of a metre down, so air gets into the peat and it slowly breaks down, giving off CO2 and some nitrous oxide. Each hectare of drained potato or wheat ground gives off about as much as the whole cattle herd does per 12 ha of peat. Put another way, 100 ha of peat gives off more than seven times the herd's methane. Wheat and potatoes come out about the same per hectare (about 37 t CO2e/ha). Potatoes give off more N2O and wheat a little more CO2 [R1, R2].

**How the options compare.** Raising the water table is the only one of the three options at the scale of your footprint. Even a partial rise under potatoes, to 0.45 m, saves about 13 times as much as the more optimistic feed-additive case. Raising it to 0.30 m roughly halves the potato ground's emissions per hectare. Rewetting to a wetland crop such as reed would cut those 60 ha by about 95% per hectare in the model. That would end potato production on that ground, so it is a change of land use, not a tweak. The feed additive is a real but modest cut, at most about 3% of the total. How well it works depends on how many days the cattle are housed and fed a ration. Hedgerow trees store carbon slowly. Their climate value on this farm is small, but they bring shade, shelter and wildlife benefits that this model does not count.

**What the model knows about your farm and what it assumes.** It does not know your actual water levels, fertiliser use or follower numbers. It uses typical Fenland values and a herd we assumed for you (see caveats). The per-hectare peat figures are in line with what the UK peat inventory reports for drained cropland. They are model estimates for a typical Fenland field, not measurements of your fields.
caveats: Not counted: the grass ground's soil (we assumed it is not deep peat; if it is drained peat, its emissions could be large), N2O from livestock manure and grazing, fuel, electricity, and bought-in fertiliser and feed. The real farm total will be higher than 4,217 t CO2e.

Peat results use a typical Fenland year and typical drainage (about 0.66 m), not your dipwells. Partial raising under potatoes assumes the water is still drawn down in summer. Whether potatoes can be grown at 0.30–0.45 m on your ground is an agronomic question the model does not answer.

The reed scenario charges N2O as if the reed were fertilised like potatoes [R5]. An unfertilised wetland crop would probably give off less N2O, so the reed savings may be somewhat understated. Methane from rewetted land is higher in the first years after rewetting.

The herd make-up was assumed: 85 calves, 20 breeding heifers, 40 steers, 20 heifers for slaughter, 2 bulls, 5 rams and 300 lambs. The methane figures use UK inventory average factors per head (Farm Carbon Calculator Tier 2), not your animals' actual weights or diets.
Feed-additive effects (15% and 30%) are our assumptions for a mainly grazing suckler herd, not results the model worked out.
The hedgerow tree numbers (100 trees on 3 km) are assumed. Growth comes from the Fens pilot tile, not your own hedges. The hedges themselves (below 3 m) are not modelled.

Water levels in the Fens are managed across whole areas through drainage boards. Raising them on one block may depend on your neighbours and the internal drainage board, and could affect the land next to you.
input.persona_section_markdown:
**Options, largest effect first**

1. **Raising water levels on the potato ground** (about 770–2,100 t CO2e/yr saved in the model). This could be a step-by-step change: keep the water higher in winter and spring under the current crops, or move part of the land to a wet crop (paludiculture such as reed or other wetland crops). It would involve sluices or weirs on your ditches and talking to the internal drainage board. You would also need to think about access, the crops you grow and your markets. Things to look into: Countryside Stewardship and Landscape Recovery options for lowland peat, SFI actions on peat soils, and the **Peatland Code**, which now covers some lowland peat. Projects under the Peatland Code commit the land for decades.
2. **Feed additive for the cattle** (about 59–118 t CO2e/yr saved). This is easiest to apply in winter when the cattle are housed and fed a ration. Check that it suits a suckler system and talk to your vet or nutritionist about cost and practicality. Results can feed into a farm carbon footprint for buyers or processors.
3. **Hedgerow trees** (about 0.4–1.0 t CO2/yr on average for 100 trees). This option is small for carbon but useful for shelter, shade for stock and wildlife. Look into SFI hedgerow actions and Countryside Stewardship capital grants for hedgerow trees.

**If you are a tenant**
- Raising water tables or changing land use on the peat is a long-term change to the holding and will almost certainly need your landlord's consent. Check whether your tenancy (FBT or 1986 Act) allows it.
- Carbon rights, and any Peatland Code or nature credits, usually belong to the landowner unless your tenancy or a separate agreement says otherwise. Agree who holds and benefits from them **before** you start.
- SFI is open to tenants who have management control for each action's duration and do not breach the tenancy. The Tenant Farming Commissioner's Code of Practice covers landlord–tenant cooperation on schemes and natural capital.
- Feed changes and hedgerow trees are usually within a tenant's control. Planting trees may still need your landlord's agreement, depending on the tenancy.

**Where to get advice:** the Rural Payments Agency and Natural England (schemes), your internal drainage board, Fenland peat and paludiculture projects run by local Wildlife Trusts and others, the Tenant Farmers Association, and a land agent for tenancy and carbon-rights questions.
next_steps: Install dipwells or share existing water-table readings. The peatland model can then be re-run with your actual water levels instead of the Fenland average.
Give the actual follower numbers and housing period so the herd methane and the effect of the additive can be recalculated.
Confirm whether the 80 ha of grass is on peat. If it is, model its soil emissions too.
Check with your landlord whether a staged water-table trial on one block of the potato ground would be acceptable.

Even a partial rise under potatoes, to 0.45 m, saves about 13 times as much as the more optimistic feed-additive case. Raising it to 0.30 m roughly halves the potato ground's emissions per hectare. Rewetting to a wetland crop such as reed would cut those 60 ha by about 95% per hectare in the model. That would end potato production on that ground, so it is a change of land use, not a tweak. The feed additive is a real but modest cut, at most about 3% of the total. How well it works depends on how many days the cattle are housed and fed a ration. Hedgerow trees store carbon slowly. Their climate value on this farm is small, but they bring shade, shelter and wildlife benefits that this model does not count.

**What the model knows about your farm and what it assumes.** It does not know your actual water levels, fertiliser use or follower numbers. It uses typical Fenland values and a herd we assumed for you (see caveats). The per-hectare peat figures are in line with what the UK peat inventory reports for drained cropland. They are model estimates for a typical Fenland field, not measurements of your fields.
caveats: Not counted: the grass ground's soil (we assumed it is not deep peat; if it is drained peat, its emissions could be large), N2O from livestock manure and grazing, fuel, electricity, and bought-in fertiliser and feed. The real farm total will be higher than 4,217 t CO2e.

Peat results use a typical Fenland year and typical drainage (about 0.66 m), not your dipwells. Partial raising under potatoes assumes the water is still drawn down in summer. Whether potatoes can be grown at 0.30–0.45 m on your ground is an agronomic question the model does not answer.

The reed scenario charges N2O as if the reed were fertilised like potatoes [R5]. An unfertilised wetland crop would probably give off less N2O, so the reed savings may be somewhat understated. Methane from rewetted land is higher in the first years after rewetting.

The herd make-up was assumed: 85 calves, 20 breeding heifers, 40 steers, 20 heifers for slaughter, 2 bulls, 5 rams and 300 lambs. The methane figures use UK inventory average factors per head (Farm Carbon Calculator Tier 2), not your animals' actual weights or diets.
Feed-additive effects (15% and 30%) are our assumptions for a mainly grazing suckler herd, not results the model worked out.
The hedgerow tree numbers (100 trees on 3 km) are assumed. Growth comes from the Fens pilot tile, not your own hedges. The hedges themselves (below 3 m) are not modelled.

Water levels in the Fens are managed across whole areas through drainage boards. Raising them on one block may depend on your neighbours and the internal drainage board, and could affect the land next to you.

**Options, largest effect first**

1. **Raising water levels on the potato ground** (about 770–2,100 t CO2e/yr saved in the model). This could be a step-by-step change: keep the water higher in winter and spring under the current crops, or move part of the land to a wet crop (paludiculture such as reed or other wetland crops). It would involve sluices or weirs on your ditches and talking to the internal drainage board. You would also need to think about access, the crops you grow and your markets. Things to look into: Countryside Stewardship and Landscape Recovery options for lowland peat, SFI actions on peat soils, and the **Peatland Code**, which now covers some lowland peat. Projects under the Peatland Code commit the land for decades.
2. **Feed additive for the cattle** (about 59–118 t CO2e/yr saved). This is easiest to apply in winter when the cattle are housed and fed a ration. Check that it suits a suckler system and talk to your vet or nutritionist about cost and practicality. Results can feed into a farm carbon footprint for buyers or processors.
3. **Hedgerow trees** (about 0.4–1.0 t CO2/yr on average for 100 trees). This option is small for carbon but useful for shelter, shade for stock and wildlife. Look into SFI hedgerow actions and Countryside Stewardship capital grants for hedgerow trees.

**If you are a tenant**
- Raising water tables or changing land use on the peat is a long-term change to the holding and will almost certainly need your landlord's consent. Check whether your tenancy (FBT or 1986 Act) allows it.
- Carbon rights, and any Peatland Code or nature credits, usually belong to the landowner unless your tenancy or a separate agreement says otherwise. Agree who holds and benefits from them **before** you start.
- SFI is open to tenants who have management control for each action's duration and do not breach the tenancy. The Tenant Farming Commissioner's Code of Practice covers landlord–tenant cooperation on schemes and natural capital.
- Feed changes and hedgerow trees are usually within a tenant's control. Planting trees may still need your landlord's agreement, depending on the tenancy.

**Where to get advice:** the Rural Payments Agency and Natural England (schemes), your internal drainage board, Fenland peat and paludiculture projects run by local Wildlife Trusts and others, the Tenant Farmers Association, and a land agent for tenancy and carbon-rights questions.

Give the actual follower numbers and housing period so the herd methane and the effect of the additive can be recalculated.
Confirm whether the 80 ha of grass is on peat. If it is, model its soil emissions too.
Check with your landlord whether a staged water-table trial on one block of the potato ground would be acceptable.

I've written the report. About 88% of your farm's modelled emissions (roughly 3,710 of 4,217 t CO2e a year) come from the drained peat under your potatoes and wheat. Raising the water table on the potato ground is by far the biggest of your three options. Many of your details weren't in the question, so I filled them with assumptions you should check (listed below).

**Where the emissions come from (t CO2e a year)**

| Source | Farm total |
|---|---|
| Potatoes on drained peat (60 ha, about 37 t per hectare) | about 2,219 |
| Wheat on drained peat (40 ha, about 37 t per hectare) | about 1,493 |
| Cattle methane | about 439 |
| Sheep methane | about 65 |
| **Total the tools could model** | **about 4,217** |

Most of the peat emissions are CO2 from the peat breaking down because it is drained, plus some nitrous oxide. Nearly all the livestock methane comes from digestion rather than manure.

**What each option would cut (t CO2e a year)**

| Option | Saving |
|---|---|
| Keep growing potatoes, raise the yearly average water table from about 0.66 m to 0.45 m below the surface | about 770 |
| Keep growing potatoes, raise it to 0.30 m | about 1,410 |
| Rewet the potato ground to grow reed, water at about 0.20 m | about 2,100 |
| Feed additive for the cattle (sheep not included) | about 59 to 118 |
| 100 hedgerow trees, averaged over 50 years | about 0.4 to 1.0 |

- **Water table:** rewetting to reed would cut emissions from that ground by about 95% per hectare, but it ends potato growing there. The model doesn't say whether potatoes would grow well with water at 0.30 to 0.45 m. The reed figure assumes potato-level fertiliser, so the real saving is probably a bit larger.
- **Feed additive:** this is at most about 3% of the farm total. The 15% and 30% cuts in cattle methane are my assumptions for a mainly grazing suckler herd, not something the model worked out.
- **Hedgerow trees:** they take up 18 to 48 t CO2 in total over 50 years. That's small for climate, but the model doesn't count shelter, shade or wildlife benefits.

**Assumptions to check:**
- **Your fields:** your peat is drained to a typical Fenland level, with 200 kg of nitrogen fertiliser per hectare.
- **Your herd:** I assumed 85 calves, 20 breeding heifers, 40 steers, 20 heifers for slaughter, 2 bulls, 5 rams and 300 lambs.
- **Your hedges:** I assumed 3 km, with one new tree every 30 m (100 trees).
- **Your grass:** I treated the 80 ha of grass as not on peat. If it is drained peat, its emissions could be large.

The real total will be higher than 4,217 t CO2e. It leaves out the grass soil, nitrous oxide from manure and grazing, fuel, and bought-in fertiliser and feed.

**As a tenant:** raising water tables or changing what you grow on the peat will almost certainly need your landlord's consent. Carbon and nature credits, such as under the Peatland Code, usually belong to the landowner unless your tenancy says otherwise. The report covers schemes to look into, the tenancy points and where to get advice.

The report has two charts, one of the emission sources and one of the savings. It is at `/home/user/slate/demo/runs/farmer/20261118-2039-your-ely-farm-where-the-emissions-come-from-and-what-three-o.html`.
